summary: Learn how language models read text by building the pieces yourself: tokenizers, word vectors, similarity search, text classifiers, entity extractors, attention, and finally a grounded document question-answering system with citations and an evaluation harness.
description: This course takes text from raw characters to grounded, checked answers, and every step is something you build and measure. You'll normalize and tokenize text, train a byte-pair-encoding tokenizer from scratch, learn word vectors from co-occurrence counts, and compare one-hot, count, TF-IDF, and embedding representations. Then you'll rank documents by cosine similarity, train naive Bayes and logistic regression classifiers on realistic support tickets, and evaluate them honestly with confusion matrices, cross-validation, and confidence thresholds. Module 4 opens up a real transformer: you'll run a named-entity model from the Hugging Face Hub, combine it with regex rules, and follow a sentence from tokens to ids to logits, then chart its attention heads. Later modules cover attention and context budgets, prompts with structured outputs and validation, retrieval-augmented generation with citations, hallucination checks, the choice between retrieval and fine-tuning, and evaluation before deployment. You work in Google Colab with scikit-learn, NumPy, matplotlib, and Hugging Face transformers. Code that runs on the lesson pages uses small datasets typed into the cell, and the output you see came from actually running it; cells that download models are marked to run in Colab, with their real output shown. Later modules can call a hosted model through the Gemini API's free tier or a local model through Ollama, and include offline stand-ins so they also work without a key. Each core module has a Notes lesson, a Build-along, and a Practice set with hints and worked solutions, and the course ends with a capstone: a grounded question-answering system for documents you choose.
audience: Strong high schoolers, early college students, and self-taught programmers who have already trained and evaluated a machine-learning model in Python and want to understand and build language systems, not just call them.
prerequisites: Python: functions, lists, dictionaries, loops, and reading a traceback
NumPy basics: arrays, shapes, indexing, and matrix multiplication
One complete scikit-learn workflow: train_test_split, fit, predict, and score
Classification metrics: accuracy, precision, and recall
outcomes: Normalize and tokenize text, train a BPE tokenizer from scratch, and explain how subword vocabularies handle words they have never seen.
Represent text as counts, TF-IDF vectors, and learned embeddings, and use cosine similarity to search and deduplicate documents.
Train and evaluate text classifiers with pipelines, cross-validation, confusion matrices, and confidence thresholds, and explain their mistakes.
Extract entities with BIO tagging, combine a transformer NER model with rules, and score extractors at the span level.
Inspect a transformer's tokens, logits, and attention weights, and explain attention, masks, and context-window limits.
Build and evaluate a privacy-aware, retrieval-grounded question-answering system that validates its output and cites its sources.

primaryTool.name: Google Colab (free) with Hugging Face transformers and scikit-learn
primaryTool.description: Colab is Google's free hosted Jupyter notebook. Python runs on a Google machine and notebooks save to your own Google Drive, so it works on any computer with a browser, Chromebooks included. transformers, PyTorch, scikit-learn, NumPy, and matplotlib come preinstalled, and models download from the Hugging Face Hub onto the Colab machine. The free CPU runtime is enough for every lesson; a free T4 GPU runtime is optional and only makes transformer cells faster.
setupSteps: Go to colab.research.google.com and sign in with a Google account (a personal account is the safe choice if your school account blocks Colab).
Choose File > New notebook in Drive, then click the Untitled name at the top left and rename the notebook.
Run the version-check cell from the first lesson; if transformers or scikit-learn is missing or too old, run %pip install -q -U transformers (or scikit-learn) and choose Runtime > Restart session.
Run the first-lesson check cell, which downloads the dslim/distilbert-NER model and confirms it finds a person and a place in a test sentence.
primaryTool.verification: The version cell prints "Ready for the course", and the check cell prints [('PER', 'Ada Lovelace'), ('LOC', 'London')] followed by "Model download and inference: OK".

optionalGear.name: Free Hugging Face account and read token
optionalGear.description: Optional. Every model in the course is public; a token stored in Colab Secrets as HF_TOKEN only raises download rate limits and unlocks gated models.

optionalGear.name: Python 3.10+ with JupyterLab on your own computer
optionalGear.description: Optional. A local install works offline and has no session limits; the first lesson has the steps for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

freeCompletionPromise: Every lesson can be completed for $0. Google Colab's free tier runs every notebook, the libraries and models are open and free to download, the datasets are typed into the lessons, and the lessons that can use a hosted language model also run with an offline stand-in, so no paid service or API key is ever required.

assignments.title: Support-ticket triage tool
assignments.brief: In a seeded Colab notebook, train a TF-IDF and logistic regression classifier on labelled support tickets, hold out a test set, prove each improvement with cross-validation, add similar-case search, and send low-confidence tickets to a human.

assignments.title: Retrieval pipeline with checked citations
assignments.brief: Chunk a small set of non-sensitive documents with overlap, retrieve with TF-IDF, pack a grounded prompt with numbered sources into a token budget, and reject any reply that fails its schema or cites a source it was never shown.

capstone.title: Grounded document Q&A
capstone.brief: Build a question-answering system over documents you're allowed to use, such as class syllabi or a club handbook: scrub and chunk them, retrieve with a measured hit rate, answer in a strict schema with citations, and abstain when checks fail.
deliverables: Colab notebook with the full pipeline
Eval set of 25+ questions, a fifth unanswerable, with a launch gate
Five-minute presentation that shows a failure
